version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm: madvise: drop MADV_PAGEOUT folios at swap writeback completion

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch improves the handling of MADV_PAGEOUT folios on asynchronous swap devices by marking them as dropbehind at isolation time instead of waiting for writeback completion. This allows the memory to be freed earlier, reducing latency and improving performance. The patch also updates various kernel modules to handle the new behavior correctly.

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer David (Arm) pointed out that the patch's behavior for MADV_PAGEOUT is inconsistent with synchronous I/O, where memory is released immediately after sync I/O completion. He argued that delaying the release until a later scan may improve swapcache hits before folios are reclaimed, but questioned whether this is relevant in practice and suggested that evicting pages as soon as possible would be more beneficial for freeing up memory.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 9/21/26 17:24, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> On an asynchronous swap device MADV_PAGEOUT only marks the folio
> PG_reclaim and rotates it to the tail of the inactive list once its
> writeback completes, so the memory is not actually freed until a later
> reclaim scan removes the by then clean swap cache folio.
But we have the same behavior when just reclaiming memory ordinarily? It's added
to the swapcache and only the next scan actually frees up the memory.

Wouldn't we memory we reclaim ... just gone, like in the sync case?

-- 
Cheers,

David

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Barry Song noted that asynchronous swap devices can experience a cold/hot inversion when rotating writeback folios to the tail of the inactive list due to fast NVMe I/O, where some pages complete writeback during isolation while others remain under writeback. He suggested skipping the later scan and reclaiming the folios immediately once the I/O completes for MADV_PAGEOUT, which is an explicit hint from userspace to reclaim memory.

On Mon, Sep 21, 2026 at 11:37 PM David Hildenbrand (Arm)
<david@kernel.org> wrote:
>
> On 9/21/26 17:24, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> > On an asynchronous swap device MADV_PAGEOUT only marks the folio
> > PG_reclaim and rotates it to the tail of the inactive list once its
> > writeback completes, so the memory is not actually freed until a later
> > reclaim scan removes the by then clean swap cache folio.
> But we have the same behavior when just reclaiming memory ordinarily? It's added
> to the swapcache and only the next scan actually frees up the memory.
>
> Wouldn't we memory we reclaim ... just gone, like in the sync case?

For synchronous I/O, such as zswap and zram, the memory is released
immediately after sync I/O is done.

For asynchronous I/O, such as NVMe, the swapcache is currently
expected to be rotated back to the tail of the LRU and wait for
another scan. Alexandre once mentioned that when he tried handling
async I/O the same way as sync I/O—releasing the memory once the I/O
completed—he saw some regression. So, delaying the release until a
later scan may allow swapcache hits before the folios are eventually
reclaimed.

But we actually have a problem here: this rotation, which puts
writeback folios at the tail of the LRU, is not reliable at all.

`folio_rotate_reclaimable()` would only work reliably if the endio
happens after the folio has been put back on the LRU head, rather than
while it is still isolated.

But nowadays NVMe is very fast. If we isolate N pages and perform
shrink on them, M pages may finish writeback during the isolation,
while the remaining N-M pages are still under writeback. M can easily
be more than 50% of N.

As a result, we can end up with the following cold/hot inversion:

LRU head
----- M pages whose writeback completed during isolation
----- other pages
----- N-M pages that are successfully rotated to the LRU tail
LRU tail

Now we can see that the M pages were expected to be reclaimed, but
they are not only left unreclaimed, but are effectively promoted to
the LRU head.

For MGLRU, commit 359a5e1416ca ("mm: multi-gen LRU: retry folios
written back while isolated") added the following code to reclaim
those M pages that finish writeback during isolation by retrying
`shrink_folio_list()` on them:

                /* retry folios that may have missed
folio_rotate_reclaimable() */
                if (!skip_retry && !folio_test_active(folio) &&
!folio_mapped(folio) &&
                    !folio_test_dirty(folio) && !folio_test_writeback(folio)) {
                        list_move(&folio->lru, &clean);
                        continue;
                }

This somehow resolves the cold/hot inversion, but leaves the M and
N-M pages with inconsistent behavior: some are actually reclaimed,
while others remain at the tail of the LRU.

For the active/inactive LRU and `MADV_PAGEOUT`, we don't have a
mechanism to restore the missed reclaim opportunity. Ridong's patch[1]
addresses this cold/hot inversion in the active/inactive LRU reclaim
path. To my knowledge, there has never been a patch to address the
same cold/hot inversion in `MADV_PAGEOUT`.

BTW, if `MADV_PAGEOUT` is an explicit hint from userspace to reclaim
the memory, would it make sense to skip the later scan and reclaim the
folios immediately once the I/O completes?

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20260920132519.3369946-1-ridong.chen@linux.dev/

Best Regards
Barry

> But we actually have a problem here: this rotation, which puts
> writeback folios at the tail of the LRU, is not reliable at all.
>
> `folio_rotate_reclaimable()` would only work reliably if the endio
> happens after the folio has been put back on the LRU head, rather than
> while it is still isolated.

I think we might better fix this instead? Or is this really a problem?
If it has PG_reclaim, it should be putback to the tail instead of
head, right?

> But nowadays NVMe is very fast. If we isolate N pages and perform
> shrink on them, M pages may finish writeback during the isolation,
> while the remaining N-M pages are still under writeback. M can easily
> be more than 50% of N.
>
> As a result, we can end up with the following cold/hot inversion:
>
> LRU head
> ----- M pages whose writeback completed during isolation
> ----- other pages
> ----- N-M pages that are successfully rotated to the LRU tail
> LRU tail
>
> Now we can see that the M pages were expected to be reclaimed, but
> they are not only left unreclaimed, but are effectively promoted to
> the LRU head.
>

> written back while isolated") added the following code to reclaim
> those M pages that finish writeback during isolation by retrying
> `shrink_folio_list()` on them:
>
>                 /* retry folios that may have missed
> folio_rotate_reclaimable() */
>                 if (!skip_retry && !folio_test_active(folio) &&
> !folio_mapped(folio) &&
>                     !folio_test_dirty(folio) && !folio_test_writeback(folio)) {
>                         list_move(&folio->lru, &clean);
>                         continue;
>                 }
>
> This somehow resolves the cold/hot inversion, but leaves the M and
> N-M pages with inconsistent behavior: some are actually reclaimed,
> while others remain at the tail of the LRU.
>
> For the active/inactive LRU and `MADV_PAGEOUT`, we don't have a
> mechanism to restore the missed reclaim opportunity. Ridong's patch[1]
> addresses this cold/hot inversion in the active/inactive LRU reclaim
> path. To my knowledge, there has never been a patch to address the
> same cold/hot inversion in `MADV_PAGEOUT`.

MADV_PAGEOUT is a bit different from the reclaim under pressure,
reclaim underpressure can easily overshoot the amount of anon folios
reclaimed, because however fast the writeback it, it can be faster by
scanning the LRU and dropping clean file folios. So before LRU
reclaimed enough clean file folios, we can't stop the reclaim.

I think the better fix is to have a separate watermark for anon / file
or a new way to handle reclaim. Reclaiming an anon folio is hardly
helpful in the short term when under heavy pressure and the device is
not a synchronous device.

The overshoot is a real issue, it's very common to see many folios
stuck in the swap cache after memory pressure. If we drop all of them,
we will see significant regressions. Treating MADV_PAGEOUT differently
here seems better.

> >>> benchmark. I'm also a little surprised by the 15% regression in
> >>> Sysbench OLTP. My initial feeling was the same as yours: we should
> >>> release the memory immediately after writeback completes, for both
> >>> synchronous and asynchronous I/O.
> >>
> >> Right. And see if we can identify why we are swapping out the wrong things :)
> >
> > I think we are not? It's about over-reclaim. In the worst case we
> > might put every anon folio under writeback, while no folio is
> > reclaimed, if the device is super slow.
> Ah, that hints at the real problem then? How confident are we that that's what's
> happening?

I'll set up this experiment again and return with numbers so we can
check what happens. I remember that at first sight, I was not able to
understand the cause of the regression so I'll need other pairs of
eyes :)

Thanks for your comments,

Alex

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH v4 5/6] btrfs: implement uncompressed fallback for delayed bbio
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where reserved space for delayed block I/O operations in Btrfs is freed twice, leading to a double free error. It introduces an uncompressed fallback mechanism to handle cases where the compressed try fails without reserving space. The approach taken involves identifying and fixing two separate problems related to reservation handling.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 01/10] selftests/mm: exercise MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds self-tests to exercise the MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT functionality in the Linux kernel. The tests cover both user-visible contracts, such as verifying that MADV_COLD does not populate PTE holes and that PAGEOUT preserves unevictable base pages, as well as implementation details like folio and page-table behavior under various scenarios. The patch includes 28 cases to test these behaviors, with some tests intentionally asserting specific conditions to detect unintended changes during a planned refactor of the page-table walker.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 06/10] mm/madvise: separate huge PMDs from the PTE walk
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the handling of huge PMDs from the PTE walk in the madvise_lru_pmd_entry function. It introduces a new helper function, madvise_lru_huge_pmd, which is responsible for handling huge PMDs and returns false when a requested split requires a PTE walk. The patch moves the lock ownership and splitting of huge PMDs into this dedicated helper, making the code more modular and easier to understand.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 07/10] mm/madvise: separate PTE-batch folio processing
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the processing of PTE-batch folios into a new helper function, madvise_lru_pte_batch_locked(). This function takes care of locking and referencing a split candidate folio before returning it to the caller. The original code combined page-table iteration with validation and processing in a single loop, which made it difficult to understand the batching rules for large folios and the ownership transferred when a partial folio is split. By moving this logic into a separate function, the patch improves the clarity and maintainability of the code without introducing any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 08/10] mm/madvise: separate the PTL-held PTE scan
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the PTE scan in the madvise function from its surrounding lock drops, allowing it to run entirely under the PTE lock. The scan is moved into a helper function that returns a locked and referenced split candidate or stops at the existing scheduling boundary. This change does not introduce any functional changes but improves the code's structure and efficiency.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 09/10] mm/madvise: make cold and pageout PTE lock ownership explicit
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the madvise_lru_pte_range_locked function to explicitly manage PTE lock ownership, making it clear who holds the lock during page-walking and huge PMD handling. The original code mixed lock ownership between the PMD callback and the page-walk callback, which is now separated into two distinct functions. This change does not introduce any functional changes but improves the clarity of the code by explicitly managing lock ownership.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 10/10] mm/madvise: share cold and pageout walk setup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the shared TLB and page-walk setup for MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT operations in the Linux kernel's mm/madvise module. It introduces a new helper function, madvise_lru_vma_range(), which is used by both entry points to perform the common setup tasks. The patch aims to reduce code duplication and improve maintainability without introducing any functional changes.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch refactors the code responsible for handling MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT page table walks to improve maintainability and auditability. The original implementation was a complex nest of functions, which led to bugs being introduced frequently. To address this issue, the patch separates the handling of huge PMDs, PTE batching, PTE-lock ownership, and shared walk setup into distinct functions. Additionally, 28 self-tests are included to ensure that the refactored code does not introduce new issues. The patch aims to simplify the control flow and make it easier to audit page-table lock ownership and split retries.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/7] mm: support promotion-only NUMA hinting scans
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces support for promotion-only NUMA hinting scans in the Linux kernel. It adds a new mode, MM_CP_PROT_NUMA_PROMO_ONLY, which allows tasks to specify that they only want to scan for pages that can be promoted to a higher-tier node. The patch also updates various functions, including folio_can_map_prot_numa and task_numa_work, to use this new mode. This change is intended to improve the performance of memory tiering systems by reducing unnecessary scans and allowing tasks to focus on promoting pages to higher-tier nodes. The patch also includes several other changes to clean up the interface and reduce complexity.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/7] sched/numa: scan read-only file mappings in tiering mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) balancing code to scan read-only file mappings when tiering is enabled, but only for promotion purposes. This change prevents hot file folios on slow memory from being promoted and ensures that shared library pages are not migrated unless it would be beneficial. The patch also updates the task_numa_work function to build protection flags for each VMA based on a snapshot of the balancing mode, ensuring consistency in PTE and PMD paths during scanning. This change addresses an issue where a binary's tier residency was not tracking its runtime hotness correctly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 4/7] sched/numa: separate VMA placement from scan continuation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the decision to place a VMA (Virtual Memory Area) for east-west sampling from the continuation of an ongoing scan across multiple scan windows. The helper function vma_is_accessed() is renamed to vma_needs_placement_scan() and its logic is split between determining placement eligibility and handling scan progress. This change allows PID-inactive VMAs to be scanned without mistakenly treating scan continuation as evidence of placement eligibility, which is a prerequisite for the next fix in this series.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 5/7] sched/numa: scan PID-inactive VMAs for promotion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) memory management to scan VMAs (Virtual Memory Areas) that are not currently active due to lack of recent PID activity. This allows for promotion-only scans, which update the VMA's previous scan sequence but do not advance the placement-starvation horizon. The patch also introduces a new field in the vma_numab_state structure to track the last completed placement scan separately from other scans. This change is intended to improve memory tiering and reduce CXL bandwidth utilization on hosts with large amounts of DRAM and CXL memory.

review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Sep 17, 2026 at 05:22:14PM +0100, Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM) wrote:
> When a user requests an mmap_action be performed in mmap_prepare, this
> involves populating the VMA range with data.
> 
> However, if the VMA is mergeable, it might then mistakenly be merged with
> another VMA without having populated the range.
> 
> Every mmap action currently available sets VMA flags such that the VMA
> cannot be merged.
> 
> However, to ensure that no future mmap action falls foul of this, assert
> that this is the case upon mmap_prepare validation.
> 
> Signed-off-by: Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM) <ljs@kernel.org>
> ---
>  mm/vma.c | 9 +++++++++
>  1 file changed, 9 insertions(+)
> 
> diff --git a/mm/vma.c b/mm/vma.c
> index d6ed10cefc8f..62f2ce1ad5a1 100644
> --- a/mm/vma.c
> +++ b/mm/vma.c
> @@ -2809,6 +2809,15 @@ static int mmap_validate(unsigned long prev_start, unsigned long prev_end,
>  int mmap_prepare_validate(const struct vm_area_desc *prev_desc,
>  			  const struct vm_area_desc *desc)
>  {
> +	/*
> +	 * It is not valid to execute mmap actions for VMAs which can be merged,
> +	 * as any such merge would leave portions of the mapping incorrectly
> +	 * unmapped.
> +	 */
> +	if (vma_flags_can_merge(&desc->vma_flags) &&
> +	    WARN_ON_ONCE(desc->action.type != MMAP_NOTHING))
> +		return -EINVAL;
> +

If you wanted to make this unit-testable, you could pull it out into a
separate function:

static bool mmap_action_is_valid(const struct vm_area_desc *desc)
{
	return desc->action.type == MMAP_NOTHING ||
		!vma_flags_can_merge(&desc->vma_flags);
}

then write:

if (WARN_ON_ONCE(!mmap_action_is_valid(desc)))
	return -EINVAL;

And you can write a unit test directly against mmap_action_is_valid

otherwise

version_history.subject: [PATCH pynfs] RPLY14: reconnect before retransmitting the call

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue in the NFSv4 client where it fails to reconnect before retransmitting a request over the same socket, which is against the RFC7530 specification. The patch introduces a new method `reconnect_same_port` that drops the current connection and reconnects from the same local port, allowing the server to see a new transport with an unchanged (address, port) cache key. This change is necessary because the client should not retry a request unless the transport connection has been broken or the procedure being retried is the NULL procedure.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch removes the ALLOC_NON_BLOCK flag from the ALLOC_RESERVES definition in the Linux kernel's page allocation code. The flag was previously used to grant access to a reserve of memory below the minimum watermark, but this caused issues when GFP_NOWAIT allocations were made under memory pressure. By removing the flag, the patch prevents direct reclaim and stalls during such bursts, ensuring that high-order atomic allocations are not disrupted by GFP_NOWAIT consumers. The patch also updates comments in the code to reflect the correct behavior of ALLOC_NON_BLOCK.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addresses David's (Arm) concern about the locking contract in collapse_single_pmd(). The author explains that the scan and run have different locking expectations, and that open-coding it in the two callers simplifies the locking rules. The author confirms that this change is necessary for moving the scan to per-VMA locking.
review_comments.raw_body:
The locking. Scan and run have different locking expectations.

I tried to explain it multiple times. Probably not well enough.
Let me reiterate.

The scan reads a PTE table under mmap_lock, fails often, and does not
drop the lock to move on to the next table.

The collapse allocates, may sleep in writeback and takes mmap_lock for
write itself, so the lock inherited from the scan is no good to it.

collapse_single_pmd() hid that boundary inside one call. It dropped the
lock somewhere in the middle, on some paths and not others, and
lock_dropped was the only way for the caller to find out.

With the two calls each has one rule: the scan runs in the caller's
locking context and never touches the lock, the run is called unlocked
and takes what it needs.

There is nothing left to report, so lock_dropped and mmap_unlocked go.
It is the same move as Nico's da98790891a4 ("require collapse_huge_page
to enter/exit with the lock dropped"), one level up.

It also makes moving the scan to per-VMA locking trivial: the caller
owns the lock and the engine never sees it. I said as much in reply to
your note on v2:

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/aqQf9hSy0iNjnL6t@thinkstation/

Patch 12 depends on it, since madvise.c gets the two calls and their
lock rules rather than a bool.

On messier: what the callers gained is an mmap_read_unlock() where they
decide to run, and what they lost is a bool telling them whether
somebody else had dropped their lock. Each caller now takes and drops
its own lock and knows it, and the engine never touches a lock it did
not take.

That is more lines at the call site and a simpler locking rules.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

> handler below? Something seems odd, as it doesn't amtch the description here.

The comment undersells it.

The flag stands in for every sub-PMD rule khugepaged applies and
MADV_COLLAPSE does not: no swapped-out PTE, no shared PTE, and
max_ptes_none scaled to the order.

Before this patch all three helpers tested is_khugepaged and then
is_pmd_order; the flag replaced the first test in each. Which makes it
is_khugepaged under another name, so you are right that it is the wrong
abstraction.

Splitting the limits works. Two sets of counts, one per order class:

	struct collapse_limits {
		unsigned int max_ptes_none;
		unsigned int max_ptes_swap;
		unsigned int max_ptes_shared;
	};

	struct collapse_policy {
		struct collapse_limits pmd;
		struct collapse_limits sub_pmd;
		...
	};

For swap and shared the sub-PMD value is a count: 0 for khugepaged, no
limit for MADV_COLLAPSE.

For none it is the knob value, and the helper keeps today's rule: 511
means all but one PTE of the window, anything else means none.

	static unsigned int collapse_max_ptes_none(struct collapse_control *cc,
			struct vm_area_struct *vma, unsigned int order)
	{
		unsigned int max_ptes_none;

		if (vma && userfaultfd_armed(vma))
			return 0;
		if (is_pmd_order(order))
			return cc->policy.pmd.max_ptes_none;

		/* Below PMD order: all but one PTE of the window, or none */
		max_ptes_none = cc->policy.sub_pmd.max_ptes_none;
		if (max_ptes_none == COLLAPSE_MAX_PTES_LIMIT)
			return (1 << order) - 1;
		return 0;
	}

its policy. MADV_COLLAPSE never reads sub_pmd: it collapses to PMD order
only. Nothing is scaled, so the creep question is untouched.

The locking. Scan and run have different locking expectations.

I tried to explain it multiple times. Probably not well enough.
Let me reiterate.

The scan reads a PTE table under mmap_lock, fails often, and does not
drop the lock to move on to the next table.

The collapse allocates, may sleep in writeback and takes mmap_lock for
write itself, so the lock inherited from the scan is no good to it.

collapse_single_pmd() hid that boundary inside one call. It dropped the
lock somewhere in the middle, on some paths and not others, and
lock_dropped was the only way for the caller to find out.

With the two calls each has one rule: the scan runs in the caller's
locking context and never touches the lock, the run is called unlocked
and takes what it needs.

There is nothing left to report, so lock_dropped and mmap_unlocked go.
It is the same move as Nico's da98790891a4 ("require collapse_huge_page
to enter/exit with the lock dropped"), one level up.

It also makes moving the scan to per-VMA locking trivial: the caller
owns the lock and the engine never sees it. I said as much in reply to
your note on v2:

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/aqQf9hSy0iNjnL6t@thinkstation/

Patch 12 depends on it, since madvise.c gets the two calls and their
lock rules rather than a bool.

On messier: what the callers gained is an mmap_read_unlock() where they
decide to run, and what they lost is a bool telling them whether
somebody else had dropped their lock. Each caller now takes and drops
its own lock and knows it, and the engine never touches a lock it did
not take.

That is more lines at the call site and a simpler locking rules.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces the virtual swap device infrastructure, allowing for dynamic allocation of swap clusters and enabling the creation of a virtual swap device that can be used by vswap. The device is capped at approximately 8 TiB in size and uses a 64-bit architecture. It includes a dynamic cluster allocator and resolves swap entries' clusters under RCU. The device is not swappable or removable and can be used by vswap-aware paths in subsequent patches.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author is addressing concerns about treating vswap as a special device due to its unique requirements and behaviors. They argue that not special casing it would lead to undesirable outcomes, such as stuck allocations and per-CPU caching issues. The author suggests that the current implementation is necessary to handle the complexities of vswap and proposes that reviewers should understand the code before proposing simplifications.

The author is addressing a concern about the swapon/swapoff interface, specifically questioning its necessity and usefulness. They express their dislike for the interface and ask the reviewer to provide a real-world use case that justifies its existence.
sentiment_signals: author asks reviewer to consider complexity
review_comments.raw_body:
This will mirror my response at [1], but I'm responding here for the
record and for your convenience.

It is needed because vswap *is* a special device, with its own
requirements. If you don't special case-it, you'd get undesirable
behaviors.

Let's take Baoquan's patch series as an example.  It treats the xswap
device as just another swap device, without any special consideration
for it. Which creates several problem:

1. At allocation time, cgroups that disable zswap might get an xswap
slot, because you don't do any check that the device you allocating
the swap slots for is xswap. At swap_writeout() time, it is *stuck* -
we already do the unmapping step, so we cannot reclaim the page.

Ironically a physical swapfile backend could have bailed us out here,
but it's not in that patch series yet :)

Vswap both has swapfile backend, AND allows you to bypass it if the
cgroup disables zswap. Both involves a bit of swap_is_vswap() check,
but I think it's worth it :)

2. Per-CPU allocation caching: since all devices share the same cache,
xswap will invalidate the caching of other devices, and vice versa. It
would be fine if the these devices are interchangeable, but as noted
above, it's not, especially without physical swapfile as the backend
option. So you're forced to taken the slow path more often.

Vswap gets around this by adding its own per-cpu allocation caching,

So by being too lazy and not carefully distinguish the swap devices,
not only does xswap not work for the writeback use case, it cannot
even work in deployments where some workloads (cgroup) select zswap,
whereas others select disk swap. It can only work if you intend to
have a single class of device - either virtual/xswap or disk swap -
but not both.

Maybe instead of just grepping for swap_is_vswap() and throw your hand
at the complexity, read the code and try to understand why it's
necessary first, then propose simplifications if you have good ideas
in minds.

---

What usecase would necessitate the need for swapon/swapoff interface?
Other than just trying to shoehorn it to an existing interface?

I've expressed why I dislike the interface in [1]. Other than the
sizing aspect, which we are already discussing in another thread,
priority also makes zero sense. You are literally exposing an
interface with only one correct answer - what's the point?

Justify your interface choice with real userspace use case, not just by
conforming to the status quo.

[1]: https://lore.kernel.org/all/CAKEwX=PEEkYiNRaVhCuM4E6mxB9huPKfkDa4m62VMTzedg1oYw@mail.gmail.com/

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 02/11] mm, swap: support zswap and zero-filled swap pages as vswap backends
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for virtual swap (vswap) using zswap and zero-filled swap pages as backends, allowing compressed or zero-filled pages to be stored without pre-allocating physical swap space. It introduces a new vswap layer that decouples PTE swap entries from physical backing, enabling efficient compression and detection of zero-filled pages. The patch also includes changes to handle virtual swap-backed entries in the zswap shrinker and writeback paths, as well as updates to mem_cgroup_can_swap() to account for vswap's contribution to memory pressure. Additionally, it introduces a new function mem_cgroup_can_vswap() to determine whether vswap is enabled for a given cgroup.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 03/11] mm, swap: prepare the swap IO path for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prepares the swap IO path for vswap by allowing it to submit IO for a swap entry other than folio->swap. It achieves this by computing the sector from an explicit entry, which is then used in various functions such as swap_add_folio and __swap_writeout. This change enables the batching path to serve both vswap entries and physical entries mapped directly into PTEs. The patch also updates ops->can_merge to measure sectors and byte offsets from the batch head plus accumulated length instead of from the previous folio plus its size.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 04/11] mm, swap: support physical swap as a vswap backend
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for physical swap as a backend for the virtual swap layer, allowing zswap to allocate physical slots on demand when it declines a page. It introduces a new mechanism to track physical slots via pointer-tagged swap_table entries and modifies readahead and swapoff operations to work with this new system. The patch also includes changes to handle cases where zswap is disabled or the folio's cgroup does not support vswap, bypassing vswap and mapping the slot directly into PTEs.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 05/11] mm, swap: enable THP swapin for vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch enables transparent huge page (THP) swapin for vswap entries, allowing large anonymous folios to be swapped in as a unit when their vswap entries share contiguous physical swap slots on a synchronous IO device. This change improves performance by reducing the number of faults and retries required during swap operations. The patch also introduces checks for zswap-backed or mixed-backing batches, which are still refused and fall back to order-0 faults. The approach taken involves modifying existing functions in the mm module to handle vswap entries and THP swapin.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 06/11] mm, swap: write back vswap zswap entries to physical swap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for writing back zswap-backed vswap entries to physical swap. It mirrors the existing zswap writeback path, but allocates the backing physical slot on demand at writeback time rather than pre-allocating it. The zswap shrinker no longer skips vswap entries unless there is no available physical swap space. The patch modifies the zswap_writeback_entry function to handle vswap entries by allocating physical backing before decompressing and storing the entry in the vtable.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 07/11] mm, swap: reclaim physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries are not being reclaimed when they become redundant. When a vswap entry's swap_count drops to 0 while its folio is still in the swap cache, the entry becomes cache-only and its physical slot is no longer needed. However, the current implementation does not properly reclaim these slots. This patch introduces a new flag, SWP_RMAP_CACHE_ONLY, to indicate when a vswap entry is cache-only, and modifies the physical reclaim scanner to reclaim such slots once swap usage exceeds 50%. The reclaimed slots are then freed, allowing for new allocations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 08/11] mm, swap: only charge physical swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies how memory charge is handled for swap entries in Linux. It ensures that only physical swap entries are charged against a cgroup's swap, rather than all swap entries including zswap-backed and zero-filled pages. This change affects the behavior of memory.swap.current and allows cgroups to reclaim their anon memory even when memory.swap.max is set to 0. The patch also refactors the swap memcg operations into separate helpers for getting, recording, charging, uncharging, and putting swap entries.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 09/11] mm, swap: add debugfs counters for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two debugfs counters to track virtual swap usage in the Linux kernel. The first counter, 'used', tracks the number of virtual swap slots (pages) currently allocated. The second counter, 'alloc_reject', counts the cumulative pages that failed to get a vswap slot. These counters are exposed under the '/sys/kernel/debug/vswap/' directory and can be accessed via debugfs. This patch addresses the need for visibility into virtual swap usage statistics, which is useful for debugging and performance analysis.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 10/11] mm, swap: defer memcg_table allocation for physical swap clusters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes memory allocation for physical swap clusters by deferring the allocation of a memcg table until it is actually needed. This reduces unnecessary memory usage in cases where a cluster only holds vswap backings, which do not require a memcg table. The patch modifies the swap_cluster_alloc_table function to allocate the memcg table eagerly only when the cluster is known to be used for direct mapping or when vswap is disabled.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v5 11/11] mm, swap: back vswap clusters with a VM_SPARSE array
series_items.patch_summary: This patch replaces the vswap cluster's individually allocated memory with a VM_SPARSE array, simplifying access and reducing overhead. The new approach eliminates per-cluster allocation, xarray nodes, and RCU grace periods, making it more efficient. The swap_cluster_info_dynamic wrapper is removed, and the virtual table for a vswap cluster is freed when it empties, reclaiming most of its memory. This change aims to improve performance and reduce memory usage in the Linux kernel's swap management.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces Virtual Swap Space (vswap), a feature that allows Linux to use a portion of physical memory as swap space, improving performance and reducing the need for disk-based swap. The patches address various issues and cleanups, including overcommit guessing, swapfile size limits, and memcg private id refcnt saturation. Additionally, they refactor swap-related operations into composable building blocks and introduce a new data structure to replace the xarray. The series also includes several bug fixes and performance improvements.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the vswap device being capped at REFCOUNT_MAX pages, which can lead to memcg private id refcnt saturation when swapping past that limit. The author explained that this is not specific to vswap and also affects physical swapfiles of similar size, but acknowledged that it's an issue worth addressing.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the OVERCOMMIT_GUESS heuristic, which gates allocations based on totalram_pages() + total_swap_pages. The author explained that vswap deliberately contributes to neither totalram_pages nor total_swap_pages, so when vswap is enabled, the bound collapses to RAM alone and allocations that vswap could absorb are refused. To fix this, the author added 2 * totalram_pages() to the OVERCOMMIT_GUESS heuristic when vswap and zswap are both on, for a 3x RAM ceiling plus whatever physical swap exists.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the swap IO path being unable to submit IO for vswap entries backed by physical slots, which identify neither the backing device nor sector. The author modified the code to compute and store the sector from an explicit entry (swap_entry_sector), allowing batching to serve both vswap and physical entries.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed concerns about the swapoff path needing to drop the per-vswap spinlock before calling try_to_unmap(), explaining that dirtying would write uninitialized memory out to swap and instead a failed read leaves the folio not uptodate, so it's dropped. The loss is now reported as SIGBUS on the next fault rather than silently returning stale data.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about zswap-backed vswap entries being rejected due to lack of physical backing, explained that the backing is checked when the folio enters the swap cache and cannot change after that, and confirmed that the issue is resolved.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern that zswap-backed and zero-filled pages were being charged against memcg->swap, which led to incorrect swap space usage tracking. The author agreed to change the charging behavior so that it occurs when a vswap entry acquires physical backing rather than at allocation. This will fix issues with memory.swap.current counting only on-disk swap usage, allow cgroups to reclaim their anon memory even if memory.swap.max is set to 0, and enable the charge to fail at writeback instead of at allocation.

>       closely follow existing patterns, move vswap backing check to
>       __swap_cache_add_check, store zero state in the swap_table for
>       vswap entries, etc.. Many of these are proposed by Kairui Song
>       in [1].
>     * Defer memcg_table allocation on physical clusters until the first
>       vswap-backing slot installs. Saves ~512 bytes per physical cluster
>       that only serves vswap-backing slots (this is the new patch 8).
>     * Widen swap_info_struct->max and ->pages (and the swapoff unuse-path
>       index) so vswap supports ~8 PB of swap space (this is the new
>       patch 9).
>     * Split the physical-swap-backend patch into three for reviewability:
>       the core backend (patch 3), zswap writeback to physical swap
>       (patch 4), and reclaim of cache-only physical slots (patch 5). No
>       functional change.
>     * Add kerneldoc for the vswap API.
>     * Add some benchmark numbers for zswap case.
> 
> 
> Patch 11 is an RFC. It swaps vswap's cluster xarray for the VM_SPARSE
> vmalloc array Baoquan He designed for xswap, to show that the data
> structure and the device model are separable: moving to his is one
> self-contained patch that adds no userspace interface. Note that
> per Baoquan's commentary (see [5]), I have skipped shrink for now, only
> freeing vtable when the cluster becomes free to minimize metadata
> overhead while keeping the skeleton in the free list. I have not done
> performance testing on this patch yet (the number is from the old design),
> but I have run a suite of simple stress tests.
> 
> It is adapted almost entirely from Baoquan's code (see [6]), so I have
> kept Baoquan's Co-developed-by and Signed-off-by tag.
> 
> 
> I. Context and Motivation
> =========================
> 
> Currently, when an anon page is swapped out, a slot in a backing swap
> device is allocated and stored in the page table entries that refer to
> the original page. This slot is also used as the "key" to find the
> swapped out content, as well as the index to swap data structures, such
> as the swap cache, or the swap cgroup mapping. Tying a swap entry to its
> backing slot in this way is performant and efficient when swap is purely
> just disk space, and swapoff is rare.
> 
> However, the advent of many swap optimizations has exposed major
> drawbacks of this design. The first problem is that we occupy a physical
> slot in the swap space, even for pages that are NEVER expected to hit
> the disk: pages compressed and stored in the zswap pool, zero-filled
> pages, or pages rejected by both of these optimizations when zswap
> writeback is disabled. This is arguably the central shortcoming of
> zswap:
> * Resource-wise, it is hugely wasteful in terms of disk usage. At Meta,
>   we size swapfile in the order of 25-50% of host RAM, depending on flash
>   availability. This is a lot of flash for a fleet of our size, and
>   with universal zswap enablement, most of this is wasted for zswap
>   entries.
> 
> * In deployments when no disk space can be afforded for swap (such as
>   mobile and embedded devices), users cannot adopt zswap, and are forced
>   to use zram. This is confusing for users, and creates extra burdens
>   for developers, having to develop and maintain similar features for
>   two separate swap backends (writeback, cgroup charging, THP support,
>   etc.). For instance, see the discussion in [2].
> 
> * Tying zswap (and more generally, other in-memory swap backends) to
>   the current physical swapfile infrastructure makes zswap implicitly
>   statically sized. This does not make sense, as unlike disk swap, in
>   which we consume a limited resource (disk space or swapfile space) to
>   save another resource (memory), zswap consumes the same resource it is
>   saving (memory). The more we zswap, the more memory we have available,
>   not less. We are not rationing a limited resource when we limit
>   the size of the zswap pool, but rather we are capping the resource
>   (memory) saving potential of zswap. Under memory pressure, using
>   more zswap is almost always better than the alternative (disk IOs, or
>   even worse, OOMs), and dynamically sizing the zswap pool on demand
>   allows the system to flexibly respond to these precarious scenarios.
> 
> * Operationally, static provisioning the swapfile for zswap poses
>   significant challenges, because the sysadmin has to prescribe how
>   much swap is needed a priori, for each combination of
>   (memory size x disk space x workload usage). It is even more
>   complicated when we take into account the variance of memory
>   compression, which changes the reclaim dynamics (and as a result,
>   swap space size requirement). The problem is further exacerbated for
>   users who rely on swap utilization (and exhaustion) as an OOM signal.
> 
>   All of these factors make it very difficult to configure the swapfile
>   for zswap: too small of a swapfile and we risk preventable OOMs and
>   limit the memory saving potentials of zswap; too big of a swapfile
>   and we waste disk space and memory due to swap metadata overhead.
>   This dilemma becomes more drastic in high memory systems, which can
>   have up to TBs worth of memory.
> 
> Swap virtualization is the answer to these issues, with three properties:
> 
> 1. Decoupled backends. For zswap in particular, this means we eliminate
>    the unused storage space, and allows zswap to be used in systems that
>    do not have enough storage capacity for physical swap (without having
>    to resort to silly hacks). Zero-filled swap pages and swap-cache-only
>    folios also benefit here.
> 
> 2. Dynamic swap space. Since virtual swap is not tied to any physical
>    resource, we can make it effectively infinite and dynamically grow it
>    on demand.
>    This massively simplifies operational provisioning, and increases the
>    utilization of compressed swap backends (zswap). Dynamicity also
>    reduces overhead on unused swap capacity.
> 
> 3. Efficient backend transfer. The virtualization scheme should not
>    introduce PTE/rmap walking overhead for backend transfer. This
>    is crucial for systems that want to support multiple swap backends
>    in a tiering fashion (for e.g zswap -> disk swap).
> 
> For more historical contexts and references, please take a look at
> the cover letter of the older vswap submissions ([3] and [v2]).
> 
> II. Design
> ==========
> 
> When vswap is enabled (via vswap=on cmdline parameter), a special vswap
> device is allocated at boot time. Anon pages that can be zswapped will
> obtain a vswap slot at swap allocation time.
> 
> These swap entries can subsequently acquire backend on-demand, such as
> a zswap entry, or a slot on a physical swap device (as a fallback option
> or at zswap writeback time).
> 
> We repurpose much of the existing swap_table infrastructure and
> swapfile allocator for this new vswap device, with two notable
> differences:
> * Clusters are dynamically allocated on demand and managed through
>   an xarray. This in turn allows us to avoid static provisioning and
>   let swap space grow dynamically.
> 
> * Each cluster of this new vswap device has a virtual_table that stores
>   the backend information of the entries in the cluster (see below).
> 
> Diagrams:
> 
>   Case 1: vswap entry (virtualized)
> 
>   PTE                  swap_cluster_info_dynamic
>   vswap_entry          +---------------------------------+
>   (swp_entry_t) ------>| swap_cluster_info (ci)          |
>                        | +----------------------------+  |
>                        | | swap_table                 |  |
>                        | |   PFN / Shadow             |  |
>                        | | memcg_table                |  |
>                        | | count,flags,order          |  |
>                        | | lock, list                 |  |
>                        | +----------------------------+  |
>                        |                                 |
>                        | virtual_table                   |
>                        | +----------------------------+  |
>                        | | NONE                       |  |
>                        | | SWAPFILE(swp_entry_t)      |  |
>                        | | ZSWAP(struct zswap_entry*) |  |
>                        | +----------------------------+  |
>                        +---------------------------------+
>                               |
>                               | SWAPFILE resolves to
>                               v
>                        PHYSICAL CLUSTER (swap_cluster_info)
>                        +--------------------------+
>                        | swap_table per-slot:     |
>                        |   NULL   - free          |
>                        |   PFN    - cached folio  |
>                        |   Shadow - swapped out   |
>                        |   Pointer- vswap rmap    |
>                        |   Bad    - unusable      |
>                        |                          |
>                        | Vswap-backing slot:      |
>                        |   Pointer(C|swp_entry_t) |
>                        |     rmap back to vswap   |
>                        +--------------------------+
> 
>   Case 2: direct-mapped physical entry (no vswap)
> 
>   PTE                  PHYSICAL CLUSTER (swap_cluster_info)
>   phys_entry           +--------------------------+
>   (swp_entry_t) ------>| swap_table per-slot:     |
>                        |   NULL   - free          |
>                        |   PFN    - cached folio  |
>                        |   Shadow - swapped out   |
>                        |   Bad    - unusable      |
>                        +--------------------------+
> 
> struct swap_cluster_info_dynamic {
>     struct swap_cluster_info ci;       /* swap_table, lock, etc. */
>     unsigned int index;                /* position in xarray */
>     struct rcu_head rcu;               /* kfree_rcu deferred free */
>     atomic_long_t *virtual_table;      /* backend info, 8 B/slot */
> };
> 
> Each vswap cluster (swap_cluster_info_dynamic) extends the classic
> swap_cluster_info struct with a virtual_table array that stores the
> backend information for each virtual swap entry in the cluster. Each
> entry is tag-encoded in the low 3 bits to indicate the backend type:
> 
>   NONE:     |----- 0000 ------|000|  free / unbacked
>   ZSWAP:    |--- zswap_entry* |001|  compressed in zswap
>   SWAPFILE: |- type:5,off:56 -|010|  on a physical swapfile
> 
> Other design highlights:
> 
> * Note that for the vswap device, we have merged the zswap xarray tree
>   with the swapfile-level clusters. This means that for zswap only users,
>   we have negligible extra space overhead.
> 
> * Both vswap entries (Case 1) and directly-mapped physical entries
>   (Case 2) coexist as first-class citizens.
> 
> * Backend transitions in the virtual_table are synchronized through the
>   swap cache and the folio lock - the same mechanism that already
>   serializes ordinary swap operations (swapin, swapout, zswap
>   writeback, swap cache reclaim). IOW, we can only assume that the
>   backend of a vswap entry is stable through swap cache/folio lock.
>   Looking at the backend without this should be done at best for
>   optimization purposes, as there is no guarantee that the backend
>   will not change under the observer.
> 
> * Pointer-tagged swap_table entries on physical clusters provide the
>   rmap (physical -> virtual) lookup.
> 
> * Virtual swap slots not backed by physical swap are not charged to
>   memcg swap counters - only physical backing is charged (I made the
>   case for this in [4]).
> 
> III. Benchmarks
> ===============
> 
> Note that the goal is not to match vswap performance with baseline on
> every single case yet - running with vswap off is still supported. We
> can optimize further once we have landed this new feature.
> 
> A. Production Workload: Instagram
> =================================
>

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH v5 01/11] mm, swap: add virtual swap device infrastructure
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch adds infrastructure for virtual swap devices, which have specific requirements and behaviors that differ from physical swap devices. Without this special casing, undesirable problems can arise, such as incorrect allocation of swap slots and per-CPU caching issues. The patch addresses these problems by adding a check to ensure that the correct device is being used for each operation, allowing for more efficient and reliable use of virtual swap devices.

review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Chris Li expressed disagreement with making vswap a special device, citing the need for xswap to be treated as a normal swap device to avoid issues like lock ordering violations and per-CPU allocation caching problems.

Reviewer Chris Li acknowledged the patch's design choice as a careful one, but noted that it usually comes with both pros and cons, indicating a neutral sentiment.

Reviewer Chris Li questioned the patch's approach to handling uncompressible pages in xswap, suggesting that xswap could store them within itself instead of rejecting them, and noted a similarity with zswap's behavior.

Reviewer Chris Li noted that xswap doesn't require a lower tier and should not need to check for swap_is_xswap(), as it lacks the baggage associated with zswap's writeback enable interface.

Reviewer Chris Li noted that the issue of swap tiering and priority is not specific to vswap, but rather a problem area in the core swap layer, which will be addressed by a separate series.

Reviewer Chris Li suggests using Baoquan's writeback series as a base for the patch, citing it as being closer to his intended design and a more suitable foundation for further development.

Reviewer Chris Li expressed disappointment that the original author did not follow his suggestion to use a proper swap_ops approach, which would eliminate the need for most of the swap_is_vswap() checks.

Reviewer Chris Li expressed concerns that the vswap patch will break existing /etc/fstab configurations, including support for UUIDs, and change user-visible behavior by enabling vswap without explicit user action. He suggested adopting a design philosophy similar to VFS-like file systems for swap, where each swap device has its own superblock.

the reclaim LRU. Zswap also stores some uncompressible pages. The last

xswap should need to have swap_is_xswap() there. Also xswap does not
have all the baggage of zswap.writeback enable interface.

This should be addressed in the core swap layer not vswap. Kairui also
has some ideas to improve that. Yes, it is a problem area, but it is
not specific to xswap. We are well aware of it and have plans to
improve it.

---

Baoquan's writeback series is out. It is by no means perfect. But it
is much closer to what I have in mind. That is a much better base to
work on.

---

Yes, I already read your code I decide that most of the
swap_is_vswap() should not be needed if taking a proper swap_ops

less."

Anyway, Baoquan's xswap writeback patch series is out. I suggest

I like universal interfaces. Your vswap will break the /etc/fstab. The
current suggestion for xswap using sysfs will break that as well.
I would like to keep the /etc/fstab interface working, including
support for UUIDs for swap devices, etc.

explicitly enabling it. That changes the previous user-visible
behavior. It breaks my mental model. Please take this feedback
seriously.

It is a different design philosophy to adopt a swap device to
implement VFS-like file systems for swap, making them swap file
systems.

file system it is. You don't get a special sysfs interface for each
different file system to create them.

flash-friendly swap file systems for example.

That is why I feel your patch series are really unclean. I dislike
special cases, I try to avoid them as much as possible.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new helper function, cgroup_account_system_time(), which charges kernel CPU time to a cgroup's cpu.stat. The function is designed to be used in conjunction with the next patch, where it will be utilized for kernel threads working on behalf of other cgroups.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/7] cgroup: add set_active_cgroup() to charge CPU time to a cgroup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function called set_active_cgroup() that allows a kernel thread to charge its CPU time to a specific cgroup instead of its own cgroup, usually root. The function sets the task's active_cgroup field and returns the old value. It first charges the time used so far to the old cgroup before setting the new active cgroup. This is necessary for tasks like memcg reclaim from a workqueue that do work for a cgroup but are not part of it. Only kernel threads in the root cgroup can call this function, and it warns and does nothing if called by other processes. The patch also adds code to charge system time to the active cgroup when set under set_active_cgroup().

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/7] psi: charge pressure to the task's active cgroup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the Pressure Stall Information (PSI) system to charge pressure to a task's active control group when it stalls, such as during memory reclaim. The active cgroup is determined by the set_active_cgroup function and updated accordingly. When the active cgroup changes, the task's pressure state is moved from the old groups to the new ones, similar to how real cgroup moves are handled. This change ensures that PSI accurately reflects the pressure on a task's current control group.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/7] sched/fair: add cfs_bandwidth_charge() for kernel work done for a cgroup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function, cfs_bandwidth_charge(), which charges kernel work done by a task to its controlling cgroup's CPU time budget. The function takes into account the cgroup's own quota and that of its ancestors with limits, ensuring that the work does not starve the group for long. If the pool cannot cover the work, it becomes debt, paid out of subsequent refills. This change is necessary to accurately reflect kernel work done by a task in the cgroup's CPU time usage statistics.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 5/7] cgroup: take set_active_cgroup() time out of the cgroup's cpu.max
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the set_active_cgroup() function to charge kernel time used by tasks to their current cgroup's cpu.max quota, in addition to updating the task's active cgroup. This ensures that CPU usage is accurately accounted for and reflected in the cgroup's statistics. The change involves storing the task's runtime at each set_active_cgroup() call and then charging the old cgroup with the used time when the active cgroup changes.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 6/7] memcg: charge high_work reclaim to the memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of high_work reclaim in the Linux kernel's memory cgroup (memcg) subsystem. When a memcg exceeds its memory.high limit, the reclaim process is currently run from a kworker thread in the root cgroup, which means it doesn't get charged to the memcg's cpu.stat or memory.pressure metrics and doesn't count against its cpu.max quota. This patch changes the reclaim process to run under set_active_cgroup(), which charges its CPU time and memory stalls to the memcg's cgroup and deducts from its cpu.max quota, providing a more accurate representation of the memcg's resource usage.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 7/7] selftests: cgroup: check that high_work reclaim is charged to the memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two selftests to the Linux kernel's cgroup testing framework. The first test, `test_memcg_high_work`, checks that high-work reclaim is charged to the memory control group (memcg) by filling its TCP receive buffers from a softirq while only one task sleeps, causing the memcg to exceed its memory limit and triggering high-work reclaim. The second test, `test_memcg_high_work_cpu_max`, runs a CPU hog in the memcg under a cpu.max limit, ensuring that the hog gets less CPU time when high-work is busy. Both tests require swap space to be enabled so that anon memory can be reclaimed.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces a mechanism to charge kernel work to the cgroup it is being done for, rather than charging it to the root cgroup. This addresses a problem where CPU time spent by kernel threads on behalf of a specific cgroup is not accounted for in that cgroup's statistics and quotas. The approach taken involves allowing kernel threads to specify which cgroup they are working for, and then updating the relevant statistics and quotas accordingly. This will improve resource isolation and accuracy of accounting for CPU usage in various scenarios, including memory reclaim from high-work queues.

review_comments.author: Tejun Heo
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Tejun Heo noted that the current approach of moving a kworker into the target cgroup before running it has scalability issues due to contention on cgroup_mutex and cgroup_threadgroup_rwsem, and suggested an alternative direction for remote charging where a kthread explicitly specifies which cgroup the work is intended for.

Reviewer noted that the proposed solution does not address net rx, another major source of displaced CPU usage, and suggested adopting an approach that can cover both memory reclaim and net rx use cases by counting per-cgroup received packets and prorating CPU consumption.

Reviewer Tejun Heo expressed concern about the unconditional forgiveness of debt capping, suggesting instead that the cgroup should be slowed down to throttle new work generation and avoid out-of-control situations, similar to IO control mechanisms.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello, Shakeel.

On Thu, Sep 24, 2026 at 11:47:04AM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:

---

This doesn't translate to net rx, which is another major source of
displaced CPU usage. Switching membership on each packet isn't going to
work there. Attribution can't happen that way. We'd much rather count
per-cgroup received packets and prorate the CPU consumption. If at all
possible, I think it'd be better to adopt an approach which can cover
both use cases.

---

I don't like the debt capping. Having debt doesn't have to mean that
the cgroup doesn't get any bandwidth at all. The cgroup just needs to
be slowed down enough that the generation of new work is throttled and
the whole thing doesn't go out of control. IO control already does
this: when IO debt is accumulated, userspace is heavily throttled, but
not completely stalled, until the whole cgroup's consumption comes
under control. I don't see why the debts would need to be forgiven
unconditionally. The cgroup can keep paying them while running at a
minimal rate to avoid triggering stall failures, and if the situation
doesn't resolve quickly, that will most likely trigger pressure based
kills in any reasonable setup anyway.

Thanks.

--
tejun

review_comments.author: Shakeel Butt (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledged a concern about accurate accounting of CPU time spent on network receive operations, particularly for modern NICs with dedicated rx queues and old NICs with shared queues. They proposed extending the mechanism to softirqs and considering a special way to account for the latter case, possibly through BPF.

Author agreed to address a concern about CPU time capping and promised to restructure it in the next patch version.
review_comments.raw_body:
Very good point. I think we need to think for net rx for two scenarios. First,
the modern NICs with rx steering support and second, old NIC with shared queues.

On the modern NICs where the workloads get their own rx queues, I think the
proposed mechanism can help to do the accurate accounting (I have to extend this
to softirqs as it is limited to kthreads atm) very easily.

The challenge you mentioned is for the old NICs where we get to know the cgroup
assosiation of the rx packets very late (or deep) in the stack. Also CPU spent
on each packet is not necessarily uniform (due to out-of-order or drops or
checksum errors or window shrinking) but for simplicity we can assume uniform
CPU. Maybe the right place to charge for such scenario might be at application
receiving those packets into the memory. I feel like we might need a very
special way to account for this case (maybe through BPF or something). At
the moment to me it seems very hard to have a universal solution which helps
this case and the reclaim case I am targetted.

If you don't mind, I think having solution for modern NICs i.e. dedicated rx
queues, should suffice for now (unless you want the solution for old NICs as
well). Let me know what you think.

---

Sounds good, I will remove this capping in the next version.

Thanks for taking a look.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 1/7] locking: add opt-in tracking of sleeping lock holders
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces an opt-in tracking system for sleeping lock holders in the Linux kernel. It allows tasks to count and report the number of locks they hold that have opted into this tracking, enabling a cheap way to check if a task is holding a lock that other tasks may be waiting for. This feature can help avoid stalls caused by memory allocation while holding shared locks, such as cgroup_mutex or kernfs_rwsem. The patch adds new APIs and infrastructure to support this feature, including a new header file and kernel configuration options.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 2/7] locking/rwsem: track holders of opted-in rw_semaphores
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a feature to track the holders of read-write semaphores (rw_semaphores) in Linux. It introduces a new flag, `tracked`, which is set when an rw_semaphore is opted-in for holder tracking. The count of holders is incremented when a task acquires the lock and decremented when it releases the lock. This feature is designed to help with debugging and troubleshooting by providing information about who holds a particular lock. It also includes support for PREEMPT_RT builds, which have a different locking mechanism. The patch modifies several kernel files to implement this new feature.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 3/7] locking/mutex: track holders of opted-in mutexes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a feature to track the holders of opted-in mutexes in Linux. It adds a function called `mutex_track_holder` that allows developers to opt-in mutexes for holder tracking. The function is used to count the number of locks held by a task, which can help identify potential bottlenecks and stalls in the system. The patch also includes changes to handle PREEMPT_RT builds and ensures that the tracking flag survives even after the lock has been released. The feature is opt-in, meaning it only applies to mutexes that have explicitly opted-in for holder tracking.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 4/7] locking/percpu-rwsem: track holders of opted-in percpu_rw_semaphores
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a feature to track the holders of percpu_rw_semaphores, which are used in various Linux kernel components such as filesystem freeze and async writes. The patch introduces a new function `percpu_rwsem_track_holder()` that allows opting-in percpu_rw_semaphores for holder tracking. It also updates several functions to count the lock holders correctly, ensuring that tasks are not preemptible while holding the lock without being counted. This feature is enabled by CONFIG_TRACK_LOCK_HOLDERS and adds a new field `tracked` to the percpu_rw_semaphore structure.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 5/7] locking/selftests: add KUnit tests for lock holder tracking
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds 16 KUnit tests to verify the lock holder tracking functionality in Linux. The tests cover various scenarios, including locks that did not opt-in, mutex and rw_semaphore calls, downgrade_write(), cleanup.h guards, nested locks released out of order, and percpu_rwsem_release()/percpu_rwsem_acquire() hand-off. Five tests use a helper thread to hold a lock and check the count, while three cases cover what the opt-in changes besides the count. The tests are designed to ensure that task_nr_tracked_locks(current) always equals the number of opted-in locks held by the task.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 6/7] Documentation/locking: document sleeping lock holder tracking
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds documentation to the Linux kernel's locking subsystem, specifically about sleeping lock holder tracking. The feature allows kernel code to identify tasks that are holding widely shared locks and may be causing stalls in other tasks waiting for those locks. It provides information on how a task can opt-in to being tracked, how the count is updated, and what it costs in terms of performance. The documentation also explains where each lock type updates the count and notes what is not covered by this feature.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 7/7] kernfs, cgroup: track holders of the cgroupfs locks
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the cgroupfs kernfs rwsems, cgroup_mutex and cgroup_threadgroup_rwsem by enabling lock holder tracking. This is done to prevent a stalled lock holder from stalling unrelated work in the cgroupfs control plane. The patch adds a new flag KERNFS_ROOT_TRACK_LOCK_HOLDERS that enables this feature for roots whose locks are shared widely across different operations, such as create, destroy and migrate. The patch also includes opt-ins for statically defined locks cgroup_mutex and cgroup_threadgroup_rwsem. This is part of a policy to read the count of lock holders, which should be implemented separately.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces a mechanism to track sleeping lock holders in the Linux kernel. It adds a count to task_struct that indicates whether a task is holding a lock that other tasks may be waiting for. patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch adds a feature to track the holders of read-write semaphores (rw_semaphores) in Linux. It introduces a new flag, `tracked`, which is set when an rw_semaphore is opted-in for holder tracking. The count of holders is incremented when a task acquires the lock and decremented when it releases the lock. This feature helps to identify deadlocks by keeping track of which tasks hold locks. The patch also includes changes to handle cases where tasks may acquire or release locks in different threads, such as with CONFIG_DEBUG_LOCK_ALLOC enabled.

version_history.subject: [PATCH 1/7] locking: add opt-in tracking of sleeping lock holders

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch introduces an opt-in tracking system to identify tasks that are holding sleeping locks, allowing the kernel to avoid stalls caused by memory allocations while holding shared locks. The system is based on each task counting the number of opted-in sleeping locks it holds, and provides a cheap way for other tasks to check if they should throttle or wait for a particular lock. Only the task itself can modify its count, eliminating the need for atomic operations. The tracking is disabled by default and only enabled when the first lock opts in.
